problem: Classic visual SLAM such as ORB-SLAM breaks down under indoor robot-navigation conditions: noisy low-frame-rate (~3 fps) narrow-FOV cameras, rapid turns (~90°/s) and featureless walls. Learned navigation systems such as Active Neural SLAM rely only on relative visual odometry, with no loop closure, so they accumulate drift. Prior learned SLAM work either learned isolated modules or only visual odometry, never a full SLAM algorithm end-to-end.
motivation: Habitat PointNav without GPS/compass under realistic sensor and actuation noise needs accurate pose estimation, since success requires stopping within 0.36 m, and it needs a map that downstream planning can use. Encoding a SLAM algorithm as a differentiable computation graph keeps the strong algorithmic prior of a particle filter (multi-hypothesis tracking, loop closing against past maps). It also lets every model component be learned for the end objective, so the features become robust to domain-specific difficulties.
key_idea: Implement the FastSLAM particle filter as an end-to-end differentiable graph (reparameterized transition sampling plus spatial-transformer map warping) and learn its mapping, transition and observation models as CNNs by backpropagating a pose-error loss through the whole algorithm.
insight: The algorithmic structure plus task-oriented learning is what matters. On Gibson traj_nav RGB-D (Table 3), the identical FastSLAM algorithm with handcrafted components gets 21.9% SR versus 77.1% with all components learned; learning any single component helps, and joint learning is best. The particle filter itself also helps: K=1 (effectively VO) gives 30.5%, versus 60.0% with only 8 particles, 77.1% with 128 and 82.9% with 512 (Table 6). Joint end-to-end finetuning is critical for RGB (8.6% → 55.2%). Learned latent map features beat supervised occupancy when occupancy prediction is hard (RGB: 23.8% occupancy-only vs 55.2% latent-only), whereas for depth, 2D occupancy suffices. Dynamically picking past maps to compare by view overlap beats a fixed last-8 window (77.1% vs 44.8%). The ORB-SLAM analysis (Table 4) shows that low frame rate is the single most damaging factor for feature tracking: ORB-SLAM goes from 3.8% to only 86.0% even under fully ideal conditions.
method: Differentiable FastSLAM backbone: K weighted particles, each a 2D pose + yaw trajectory. The global map is a collection of per-step local maps whose local-to-global transform depends on the particle trajectory. The pose estimate is the weighted mean of particles, and a global occupancy grid is built by warping local maps along the mean trajectory. The implementation is built on PF-net (TensorFlow).

Mapping model: a fixed perspective transform maps the 160×90 RGB or depth image to a 160×160 top-down view, then CoordConv CNNs output a 40×40×Nch local map (12 cm cells, 4.8×4.8 m). Configurations are 16 latent channels (RGB), or latent + occupancy (RGB-D, depth only as input). An extra visibility channel is included. RGB occupancy uses the ANS ResNet-18 conv-dense-deconv network.

Transition model: a CNN on (o_t, o_{t-1}, o_t − o_{t-1}) outputs a Gaussian mixture (k=3) per discrete action and per x/y/yaw coordinate. It is pre-trained by maximum likelihood on relative poses, and samples are drawn with the reparameterization trick so gradients pass through.

Discriminative observation model: a CNN scores the compatibility of the current local map with a past local map, after warping the past map into the current frame by the particle's relative pose using a spatial transformer. The per-particle log-weight is the sum over pairs. Pairs are the last 4–8 steps in training and 8 steps chosen dynamically by estimated view overlap at inference. Weights are multiplied by the exponentiated score and normalized.

Multi-stage training: (1) pre-train the transition model; (2) pre-train mapping+observation for the end objective using GT motion with small Gaussian noise; (3) jointly finetune everything with Huber loss on 2D position + 1D orientation error, freezing the transition conv layers and GMM head and any occupancy-supervised mapping net. Training uses 4–8-step trajectories and K=32 without resampling; inference uses full trajectories with K=128 and resampling every step.

Navigation pipeline (like ANS but SLAM-net in place of VO): a weighted D* planner runs on the thresholded (p>0.5) 8-connected grid with obstacle-distance costs, replanned every step. A local controller turns or moves toward the furthest straight-line traversable path point. Collision recovery triggers when the pose changes <3 cm after a forward action: an obstacle is registered, then 6 turns and 1 step back. A hard-coded initial spin runs until the estimated rotation exceeds 370°.

setting.training_data: Habitat Gibson: 72 training scenes, 36k navigation episodes (500/scene) rendered as image-pose trajectories from a policy alternating shortest-path expert (30 steps) and random actions (40 steps), plus GT occupancy maps for pre-training the mapping model. Supervision uses GT 2D poses. A separate model is trained on KITTI raw for the KITTI experiments.

The SLAM localization benchmarks are the authors' own generated trajectories with SR defined as final pose error < 0.36 m.
results: In noisy Habitat Gibson conditions, SLAM-net localizes with 83.8% SR / 0.16 m RMSE (RGB-D, expert trajectories). Baselines on the same data: learned VO 60.0%, handcrafted FastSLAM 21.0% and ORB-SLAM 3.8%; ORB-SLAM fails completely with RGB. SLAM-net transfers without retraining to Replica (78.8%) and Matterport (49.5%). Plugged into a D* navigation pipeline, it reaches 64.5% SR / 0.377 SPL on the Habitat Challenge 2020 PointNav leaderboard, beating the prior best VO entry (37.3% / 0.266) and the challenge winner Occupancy Anticipation (29.0% / 0.220). On KITTI driving, however, it is far worse than ORB-SLAM (83.5 m vs 7.62 m RMSE on seq 09).
limitations: Designed for planar indoor motion with 2D local maps near the camera and no dedicated particle proposal for closing large loops. It performs much worse than ORB-SLAM on long, high-quality KITTI driving trajectories, where it overfits because of limited training data.

Training is memory-bound: it uses only 4–8-step trajectories and 32 particles without resampling. The model overfits to training conditions, e.g. more than 8 map comparisons at inference does not help.
Evaluated only in simulation (Habitat) with task-specific learned features that may be less reusable across tasks; real-robot deployment is left to future work.
